title: #25 Shift when you ask students to copy things down
author: Craig Barton
summary: In this Tips for Teachers issue, Craig Barton offers a compromise position on copying worked examples. He starts from his earlier argument that having students copy objectives, worked examples and corrections may waste lesson time and hurt learning, but accepts that the practice is too ingrained to drop outright. His proposal is a smaller change: move the copying to later in the lesson. The reasoning is that students are usually asked to copy an example at exactly the point where it makes least sense to them, having seen the concept modelled only once and with no sense of whether they can follow each step, so the copying is passive. Instead, the teacher models as normal, leaves the working visible, and has students practise first. Only then do students copy an example, now annotating each step for their future selves, which turns copying into sense-making and can serve as the lesson's plenary.
points: Barton's diagnosis: the conventional moment for copying a worked example is the point at which students understand it least.
Copying straight after a single modelled example is passive because students cannot yet judge whether they can get from one step to the next.
His fix keeps the modelled working on the board (or printed) as a reference while students practise the procedure first.
Delayed copying lets students annotate each step for 'their forgetful future self', turning transcription into sense-making that can double as a plenary.
quotes: A few weeks ago, I wrote a post for my Eedi newsletter entitled The Myth of Copying Things Down. I argued that asking students to copy lesson objectives, worked examples and corrections in their books might be both a waste of precious lesson time and detrimental to learning.

However, I know that copying worked examples is so ingrained in many teachers’ practice - and, as a result, in students’ expectations - that it is going to be hard to break away from. So here, I want to suggest a smaller change: shift the time we ask students to copy a worked example to later in the lesson.

The point at which most teachers ask students to copy a worked example into their books is the point at which the worked example makes the least sense to them. Students are likely to have just watched the teacher model this novel concept a single time.

They have no further experience of the concept, and hence no real sense of whether they possess the knowledge to get from step 1 to step 2, step 2 to step 3, and so on. As a result, copying a worked example is likely to be a relatively passive experience.

Instead, we could model the worked example as normal and leave our working up on the board so it is visible to students in case they wish to refer to it. The example could be printed out if needed. We then ask our students to practice the procedure, gaining confidence, experience and knowledge.

Because this example has more meaning attached to it, we can ask students to add notes and annotations around their working out to help their forgetful future self understand each of the steps involved. They are no longer passively copying down, but sense-making.
